# Additions to Daniel — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Multiple unknown authors; possibly composed in Hebrew/Aramaic, surviving in Greek |
| **Date** | c. 200–100 BCE for the compositions; Greek text by 100 BCE |
| **Audience** | Jews under Hellenistic pressure; later, Christian liturgical communities |
| **Genre** | Liturgical prayer and hymn; judicial thriller; satirical court narrative |
| **Timeline** | Set in the Babylonian exile (6th century BCE); composed centuries later |
| **In One Sentence** | Three additions to the Greek Daniel — a pair of liturgical hymns inserted into the fiery furnace story, a brilliant courtroom tale about a falsely accused woman, and a satirical takedown of Babylonian idol worship that ends with the lions' den — together complete the portrait of Daniel as the paradigmatic faithful Jew who triumphs over the corruptions of empire through prayer, shrewdness, and uncompromising integrity. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Book of Daniel in the Hebrew/Aramaic canon tells stories about Jews in the Babylonian court and contains apocalyptic visions, and in every version it has been one of the most read, argued over, and imaginatively fertile texts in the Bible. But the Greek Daniel — the version that circulated among Diaspora Jews and then in the early Christian church — is considerably richer. Three substantial additions appear in the Greek tradition that have no counterpart in the Hebrew/Aramaic Daniel: a prayer and hymn inserted into the fiery furnace story (Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men, corresponding to the narrative gap in Daniel 3), and two complete stories appended to the book (Susanna and Bel and the Dragon).

All three additions were composed in what appears to be the Maccabean period or slightly earlier — the second century BCE — though the exact dating of each is debated, and some scholars argue for Hebrew or Aramaic originals behind the Greek. Origen, the third-century Church Father who produced a critical edition of the Greek Bible, noted that the additions were absent from the Hebrew Daniel and marked them accordingly. Jerome, translating the Vulgate, included them while acknowledging their disputed status. They have been read in Christian communities continuously from the second century to the present.

The three additions are quite different from each other in character, and understanding them together requires recognizing that they are not a unified composition. The Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men is primarily liturgical — its purpose is doxological, not narrative. Susanna is a masterpiece of courtroom drama, a text that depends for its effect on structural irony and the careful withholding of information. Bel and the Dragon is comic detective fiction with a polemical edge. That these three texts came to be gathered with Daniel is due partly to thematic affinity (they all involve Daniel or his companions in contexts of imperial threat and divine deliverance) and partly to the practical logic of textual transmission — once someone decided they belonged with Daniel, they stayed with Daniel.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

**Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men:** The Hebrew/Aramaic Daniel 3 has a peculiar gap in it. After the three young men are thrown into the furnace (v. 23), the narrative says nothing about what happened inside the furnace until the king looks in and sees them walking around with a fourth figure (v. 91 in the Greek versification, v. 25 in English). The Hebrew text says nothing about what the three did or said during this interval — an interval of silence that cries out for content. The Prayer of Azariah fills this gap with a penitential prayer (offering the community's suffering as a sacrifice since the Temple has been destroyed) and the Song of the Three Young Men fills it with one of the most magnificent praise hymns ever composed in the Jewish tradition: a responsive canticle calling on all creation — heavens, waters, angels, sun and moon, rain and dew, mountains, every creature of the sea — to bless and praise the God who has delivered them from the fire.

The Song (also called the Benedicite, from its Latin opening word) was adopted into Christian liturgy within the first few centuries CE and has been sung or recited in Christian worship continuously for roughly 1700 years. It appears in the liturgies of the Roman Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, and the Church of England's Book of Common Prayer. It is not hyperbolic to describe it as one of the most influential texts in the history of Christian worship.

**Susanna:** The Susanna story is almost certainly the earliest surviving example of what we would call a detective story — a narrative whose plot depends on the withholding of crucial evidence, a false accusation, and a brilliant cross-examination that reveals the truth. Two elders, men of position and power in the Jewish exile community, observe the beautiful Susanna bathing in her garden and attempt to coerce her into sex by threatening to accuse her of adultery with a young man if she refuses. She refuses. They make their false accusation. The community believes them — because they are elders, because their word carries institutional weight. Susanna is condemned to death. Then the young Daniel intervenes, demands the witnesses be separated and cross-examined, and exposes the contradiction in their testimony: one says she was under a mastic tree; the other says an evergreen oak. The perjury is exposed. The elders are executed. Susanna is vindicated.

The purpose of this story is layered. At the surface level it is a story about judicial corruption — about the way institutional authority can be weaponized against the innocent, and about the vulnerability of anyone (especially women) who depend on institutions controlled by men who can lie. At a deeper level it is a story about divine justice working through human cleverness: Daniel's inspiration is described as the spirit of God moving him, but the method is entirely rational — separating witnesses and asking them the same question is a technique any competent judge could use. At a still deeper level, the story is about the courage of a single voice interrupting a social consensus built on lies: "I will not do it," Susanna says when the elders threaten her (v. 23), and that refusal in the face of certain death is the moral center of the narrative.

**Bel and the Dragon:** Two stories in one brief text, both involving Daniel exposing the fraud of Babylonian idol worship. In the first (Bel), the king invites Daniel to worship before the statue of Bel, whose priests claim the statue consumes enormous quantities of food each night — proof that the god is alive. Daniel scatters ashes on the temple floor at night; in the morning, footprints reveal the priests and their families sneaking in through secret doors to eat the offerings themselves. The fraud is exposed; the priests are executed; the idol is destroyed. In the second story (the Dragon), the Babylonians worship a living dragon, which they claim is an authentic living god. Daniel feeds it a mixture of pitch, fat, and hair pressed into cakes; the dragon eats them and explodes. The Babylonians, furious, throw Daniel into the lions' den for a second time; the prophet Habakkuk is miraculously transported from Judea to feed him; he survives; the king is converted. Both stories are, at bottom, the same argument as the Letter of Jeremiah but delivered in narrative form: the thing you worship is not a god. Here is the evidence. Here is the proof. Now watch while it is destroyed.

---

## How to Read This Book

**Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men:** Read Daniel 3 in the Hebrew versification up through verse 23, then insert and read the Prayer and Song before continuing with verse 24. This is how the text was designed to be read, and the insertion dramatically transforms the experience of Daniel 3. What in the Hebrew text is a narrative gap becomes, in the Greek version, a sustained meditative interlude: the three young men are in the fire, and instead of waiting in silence for the king to look in, the reader accompanies them inside the furnace where they are praying. The shift from narrative suspense to liturgical praise is deliberately disorienting — and then the Song, as it calls on the entire cosmos to join the praise of the God who delivers the faithful from fire, sweeps the reader into something vast that transcends the particular situation of three men in a furnace.

The Song of the Three Young Men is structured as a responsive canticle with a refrain: "Praise him and highly exalt him forever." It proceeds through the entire cosmos systematically — heavens, angels, waters, sun, moon, stars, rain, wind, fire, heat, cold, dew, nights, days, light, darkness, ice, snow, mountains, hills, all things growing, seas and rivers, whales and creatures of the waters, birds of the air, beasts and cattle, people of Israel, priests, servants of the Lord, righteous ones, humble and holy ones. The effect is cumulative and, read aloud in community, genuinely overwhelming. This is cosmic praise poetry of the highest order.

**Susanna:** Read it as a thriller. The author withholds the key information — that the elders are lying — long enough to build genuine narrative anxiety. The initial description of Susanna is elegantly balanced: her beauty, her piety, her parents' righteousness, her husband's wealth. The elders' desire for her is described with uncomfortable intimacy; the author does not sanitize it or make them cartoon villains. They are recognizably human in their failure. The confrontation scene (vv. 19–23), in which they present Susanna with an impossible choice and she chooses integrity over survival, is the moral crux of the entire story and deserves to be read slowly.

Daniel's cross-examination is brief and precise — a model of focused questioning. The question he asks is seemingly trivial: what kind of tree? The contradiction it reveals is fatal. A modern reader might note that the specific trees named are chosen for a pun in Greek: "mastic tree" (schinos) / "cut him in two" (schisai), and "evergreen oak" (prinos) / "cleave him asunder" (prisai). This wordplay is present only in the Greek text; it disappears in translation. The author was a careful literary craftsman.

**Bel and the Dragon:** Read it as satirical comedy. The tone is lighter than any other part of Daniel — the exploding dragon, the ashes on the temple floor, the footprints of the priests' children, Daniel's cheerful insolence before the king ("I worship the Lord my God, for he is the living God," v. 5) — all of it has the register of a story being told with a wink. The Habakkuk episode (vv. 33–39) is the most fantastical moment in all of Daniel, more so than the fiery furnace or the lions' den, and it may have been designed to function as comic relief: the prophet seized by the hair of his head, transported through the air to Babylon, delivered his lunchbox to Daniel in the lions' den, and then immediately whisked back to Judea.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

**Daniel 3 (fiery furnace narrative):** The Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men exist entirely within the context of Daniel 3. Reading them without knowing Daniel 3 misses all the drama that makes the hymn's praise so charged. The three young men are in the fire when they sing "Praise him and highly exalt him forever." The fire is the context. The praise is the response to the fire. This is the theology of the entire canonical Daniel in miniature: the faithful person, in the worst situation imaginable, praises God.

**Psalm 136 (great responsive praise psalm):** The Song of the Three Young Men's responsive structure — each line ending in the same refrain — is formally identical to Psalm 136, the great "his steadfast love endures forever" psalm. Both texts use the refrain as a congregational response. Both move through creation and history. Reading them together suggests they belong to the same liturgical tradition of responsive cosmic praise.

**Isaiah 44 and Letter of Jeremiah (idol polemic):** Bel and the Dragon is the narrative version of what Isaiah 44 and the Letter of Jeremiah argue in polemic and satire. All three texts are making the same point: the idols are frauds. Isaiah 44 makes it by analyzing the manufacturing process; the Letter of Jeremiah makes it by cataloguing idol helplessness; Bel and the Dragon makes it by showing a detective exposing the priests who perpetuate the fraud.

**Susanna and Joseph (the falsely accused righteous one):** The structural parallel between Susanna and the Joseph cycle is exact: a beautiful, faithful person attracts desire they did not seek, refuses to sin, is falsely accused by those whose advances they rejected, is condemned on fabricated evidence, and is finally vindicated by God working through human intelligence. Joseph's accuser is a woman (Potiphar's wife); Susanna's accusers are men. The inversion is deliberate and pointed.

**Susanna and the Gospel of John 8 (the woman brought before judges):** The story in John 8 of the woman caught in adultery — brought before Jesus by scribes and Pharisees who want to use her as a theological trap — has suggestive parallels with Susanna. Both stories involve a woman accused of sexual sin by men whose motivations are, at least in part, self-interested. Both stories involve a dramatic intervention that exposes the accusers' moral failure. Whether the author of John 8 knew the Susanna story is debated, but the resonances are real.

**The Benedicite and Christian liturgy:** The Song of the Three Young Men is one of the texts that most deeply connects the deuterocanonical tradition to the living practice of Christian worship. It was used in Eastern Christian liturgy from at least the 4th century, incorporated into the Rule of St. Benedict (6th century) as a regular canticle for Sunday Lauds, included in the Book of Common Prayer (1549 and all subsequent editions), and is still sung in the liturgy of the hours in Roman Catholic, Orthodox, and Anglican traditions. A Christian who has attended any formal liturgical worship has very likely sung or recited this text without knowing its origin.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The insertion point of the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men within Daniel 3 is not obvious to a reader encountering the additions in isolation at the end of a Bible. The additions belong inside the furnace story — between verse 23 and verse 24 of Daniel 3 — and the experience of the text is completely different when read in that position. The Hebrew text's conspicuous silence during the interval inside the furnace is what created the space for the additions; reading the additions outside that context makes them feel like appendices rather than the interpretive center they are.

The Susanna story's placement in the textual tradition is also confusing. In the Greek Septuagint (Theodotion recension, which became the standard), Susanna appears as chapter 13 of Daniel — after the apocalyptic visions of chapters 7–12. In the Old Greek Septuagint (the older translation), Susanna appears before Daniel 1, as a prologue introducing the young Daniel. The placement matters: as a prologue, it introduces Daniel as a youth who already possesses prophetic wisdom; as an appendix, it is one more example of Daniel's gifts applied in a new context. Most modern English translations follow the Theodotion placement.

The exploding dragon in Bel and the Dragon (v. 27) is one of the great unsung moments of ancient comedy. The visual is unmistakable: Daniel, asked to bow before a living dragon, feeds it homemade cakes that cause it to swell and burst. The author clearly found this funny. The story is making a serious point — living creatures worshipped as gods are no more truly divine than statues — but it is making it with considerable relish. Treating Bel and the Dragon as solemn theology misses the author's register entirely.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Additions to Daniel are absent from the Hebrew/Aramaic Daniel — and therefore from the Protestant Old Testament — for the same structural reason as all other deuterocanonical texts: they do not appear in the Hebrew manuscript tradition. The Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men, Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon are attested only in Greek (and in the versions translated from the Greek: Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic). Whether they were composed in Greek or translated from Semitic originals that did not survive is debated, but no Hebrew or Aramaic manuscripts of any of the three additions have been recovered.

Origen noticed their absence from the Hebrew Daniel in the third century CE and marked the additions in his Hexapla (his six-column comparison of Old Testament versions) with critical notation. Jerome, translating the Vulgate, included them while acknowledging they were not in the Hebrew. He gave the additions their canonical position (Prayer of Azariah/Song of the Three within Daniel 3; Susanna as chapter 13; Bel and the Dragon as chapter 14) that Catholic Bibles still follow.

Protestant reformers excluded the additions along with other deuterocanonical material. The result is that Protestant Bibles contain a twelve-chapter Daniel, while Catholic and Orthodox Bibles contain a fourteen-chapter Daniel with material inserted into chapter 3. The Song of the Three Young Men — despite being absent from Protestant Old Testaments — has never left Christian liturgical practice in the churches that use a liturgy of the hours, giving it a continuous worship history of roughly 1700 years that makes it one of the most durably used texts in the entire Christian tradition.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 605–535 BCE | The Babylonian exile — the fictional setting for Daniel and its additions |
| c. 167–164 BCE | Maccabean revolt; canonical Daniel's visions composed in this period |
| c. 200–100 BCE | Probable composition period for the three additions |
| c. 100 BCE | Greek Daniel (with additions) in wide circulation; Theodotion recension in use |
| c. 230 CE | Origen's Hexapla notes the additions' absence from Hebrew Daniel |
| c. 382–405 CE | Jerome's Vulgate: includes additions in Daniel 3, 13, and 14 |
| c. 400–500 CE | Song of the Three Young Men incorporated into Eastern Christian liturgy of the hours |
| 529 CE | Rule of St. Benedict prescribes the Benedicite (Song of the Three) for Sunday Lauds |
| 1549 CE | Book of Common Prayer includes Benedicite as an authorized alternative canticle |
| 1546 CE | Council of Trent defines Additions to Daniel as deuterocanonical for Roman Catholics |
| 1611 CE | King James Bible Apocrypha includes the additions; Protestant Daniel remains 12 chapters |
| Present | Benedicite sung in Roman Catholic, Orthodox, and Anglican liturgical traditions worldwide |
